key_cases.case_name: Knox v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination and held that under Code § 16.1-283 a court need make no separate finding of parental unfitness, because a finding of the statutory factors plus the child's best interests is itself equivalent to a finding of unfitness.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Virginia statement of what a court must find to terminate: best interests plus the enumerated § 16.1-283 factors, with no additional unfitness finding required.
key_cases.quote: In our opinion, a finding that the factors exist is tantamount to a finding of parental unfitness.

key_cases.case_name: Toombs v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(C)(2), holding that whether parental visitation must continue after a termination petition is filed is decided case by case with the child's best interests as the guiding principle, and that clear and convincing evidence supported the statutory factors here.
key_cases.relevance: It is the companion case applying the § 16.1-283(C)(2) clear-and-convincing standard to affirm termination.
key_cases.quote: The question must be resolved, however, in light of the facts of each case, with the best interests of the child as the guiding principle.

key_cases.case_name: Christopher Farrell v. Warren County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination and rejected the father's due process challenge, holding that Code § 16.1-283(B) is constitutional because the Department must prove every element supporting termination by clear and convincing evidence even though the underlying abuse or neglect adjudication uses a preponderance standard.
key_cases.relevance: This is Virginia's leading published rejection of a constitutional attack on the § 16.1-283(B) termination scheme, confirming clear and convincing proof of unfitness is required.
key_cases.quote: In the context of terminating a parent’s rights, the Due Process Clause requires that the Department prove each of the necessary allegations of parental unfitness by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.case_name: Adam Yafi v. Stafford Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(E), holding that where a parent is convicted of felony child abuse causing serious bodily injury to a sibling or subjects a child to aggravated circumstances, the Department need not prove it offered reasonable and appropriate rehabilitative services.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading published Virginia authority on the § 16.1-283(E) aggravated-circumstances route to termination, including for an incarcerated parent.
key_cases.quote: the termination of Yafi’s residual parental rights under Code § 16.1-283(E)(iii) and 16.1-283(E)(iv) did not require a predicate showing that DSS provided any services to Yafi

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reinstated the adoption decree, holding that Virginia's adoption statutes satisfy Fourteenth Amendment due process because the Code § 63.2-1205 factors require consideration of parental fitness and the effect on the child, so courts may not graft an additional judicially created 'detriment to the child' finding onto the statute.
key_cases.relevance: It is the governing Virginia statement of the constitutional floor for adoption over a birth parent's withheld consent.
key_cases.quote: Rather, for these statutes to pass constitutional due process scrutiny, they must provide for consideration of parental fitness and detriment to the child.

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed a decree allowing a stepfather to adopt over the natural father's objection and dismissed the adoption petition, holding that although the child's welfare is of paramount concern, the condition applicable in parent versus non-parent custody contests applies equally in adoption cases.
key_cases.relevance: This is the foundational Virginia rule for adoption over a natural parent's withheld consent and the doctrinal predecessor of both Doe v. Doe and Copeland v. Todd.
key_cases.quote: The condition is that the rights of parents may not be lightly severed but are to be respected if at all consonant with the best interests of the child.
